usage: 식사하다 is the verb; 를 marks the meal as object
subject 가 — the meal itself is delayed
examples: casual invite; 식사하다 fuses noun + 하다
compliment to the cook; past tense
standard polite greeting up the hierarchy
nuance: 식사 食事 (literally 'eat-affair') is the dignified, Sino-Korean word for a meal, while 밥 is the plain native word that also literally means cooked rice. The dividing line is register, not meaning: with friends or children you say 밥 먹었어? but to a boss, an elder, or a customer you switch to 식사하셨어요?, which sounds respectful and adult. 식사 pairs naturally with 하다 (식사하다), 준비하다, 대접하다 (treat someone to a meal). The classic English-speaker pitfall is reaching for the verb 식사를 먹다; Korean treats 식사 as an activity, so you either say 식사하다 or, more plainly, 밥을 먹다 — never 식사를 먹다.

밥 is the plain native word that also literally means cooked rice. The dividing line is register, not meaning: with friends or children you say 밥 먹었어?, but to a boss, an elder, or a customer you switch to 식사하셨어요?, which sounds respectful and adult.

mistakes: Saying 식사를 먹어요. 식사 already implies eating, so it takes 하다: 식사해요, or use 밥을 먹어요 instead.
Greeting a close friend with 식사하셨어요? — it sounds stiffly formal; with peers say 밥 먹었어?
Treating 식사 as countable like 'three meals'. Koreans count meals with 끼: 하루 세 끼 (three meals a day), not 세 식사.

usage: 넣다 = put in; 을 marks the salt
subject 이 — the food is over-salted
조금 = a little, softens the amount
examples: I add a little salt to the soup.
cooking action with 에 (into the soup)
This food is a bit salty.
describe taste with 짜다, not 소금이 많다
If it's bland, add more salt.
nuance: 소금 is plain native-Korean table salt, the baseline seasoning whose taste is 짜다 (salty). Don't confuse the substance with the flavor: the food is described as 짜요 (salty) or 싱거워요 (bland/under-seasoned), while 소금 is the thing you add to fix bland food. Its constant opposite in the kitchen is 설탕 (sugar), and the two look and pour alike, which is exactly the running joke when a cook grabs the wrong jar. 소금 collocates with 넣다, 뿌리다 (sprinkle), 치다 (toss salt on), and 간을 하다 (season to taste). The English-speaker trap is the particle on requests: say 소금 좀 주세요, not 소금을 주세요 with full force — the bare 소금 + 좀 sounds far more natural and polite at a table.

usage: 넣다 = put in; 을 marks the sugar
but for taste prefer the adjective 달다
I add a lot of sugar
많이 = a lot, adverb before the verb
examples: I add sugar to the coffee.
에 marks the drink it goes into
저는 단 거 별로 안 좋아해요.
I don't really like sweet things.
express preference with 단 거, not 설탕
describe taste with 달다, not 설탕이 많다
nuance: 설탕 雪糖 (literally 'snow-sugar', for its white crystals) is refined white sugar; the taste it gives is 달다 (sweet). As with salt, separate the substance from the flavor — food is 달아요 (sweet), and 설탕 is what makes it so. Korean savory cooking quietly uses a spoon of 설탕 to round off salty-spicy sauces, so 설탕 is a normal pantry item, not just for dessert. Its kitchen partner-opposite is 소금, and it collocates with 넣다, 뿌리다, and 타다 (dissolve sugar into a drink). A frequent English-speaker pitfall: to say a dish 'is sweet' use 달아요, not 설탕이 많아요, which oddly reports the ingredient amount rather than the taste.

Forgetting 없이 takes no particle: it's 설탕 없이, never 설탕을 없이.

usage: 넣다 = add; 을 marks the sauce
I dip it in soy sauce
찍다 = dip; 에 marks the dipping target
examples: I dip the dumplings in soy sauce.
This soy sauce is a bit salty.
I add a spoonful of soy sauce to the dish.
nuance: 간장 (the 간 here is the native root meaning 'saltiness/seasoning', not a hanja for liver) is dark fermented soy sauce that delivers a deep savory saltiness plain 소금 can't reach. Two real types matter in a Korean kitchen: 국간장 (light, for seasoning soups) versus 진간장/양조간장 (darker, for stir-fries and braises and as a dip), so 'soy sauce' is really a small family. It collocates with 찍다 (dip), 넣다, 붓다, 조리다 (braise in soy sauce), and 졸이다. The English-speaker pitfall is the dipping particle: you dip food INTO sauce with 에 — 간장에 찍다 — not 간장을 찍다; and note 붓다 is ㅅ-irregular, dropping the ㅅ to give 부어요.

Conjugating 붓다 as 붓어요. It is ㅅ-irregular: 부어요 (pour).

usage: 넣다 = add; 을 marks the paste
I mix it with chili paste
비비다 = mix; 에 marks what you mix into
examples: I add chili paste to bibimbap.
에 marks the dish it goes into
This chili paste is really spicy.
I mix rice with chili paste and eat it.
nuance: 고추장 (고추 'chili pepper' + 장 醬 'fermented paste') is thick red fermented chili paste — spicy 맵다 but with an underlying sweetness and fermented depth, so it isn't just 'hot'. Keep it apart from its jar-mate 된장 (brown soybean paste, savory not spicy) and from 고춧가루 (dry chili powder); all three live in Korean cooking but do different jobs. 고추장 collocates with 비비다 (mix into rice), 넣다, 풀다 (dissolve into stew), and 찍다 (dip lettuce/cucumber). Two conjugation traps hide here: the partner verbs 맵다 (→ 매워요, ㅂ-irregular) and 바르다 (→ 발라요, 르-irregular) both shift stems, and you mix rice 고추장에 비벼요 with 에, not 고추장을.

mistakes: Treating 고추장 and 된장 as the same paste. 고추장 is red and spicy; 된장 is brown, salty-savory soybean paste.
Saying 맵어요. 맵다 is ㅂ-irregular, so it becomes 매워요.
Confusing 고추장 (the paste) with 고춧가루 (dry chili powder) — different texture and use.

examples: Mom makes stew with soybean paste.
으로 marks 된장 as the means
This soybean paste is a bit salty.
I dissolve soybean paste into the broth.
풀다 = stir paste until it spreads
nuance: 된장 (된 'thick/stiff' + 장 醬 'fermented paste') is brown fermented soybean paste with a deep, salty, almost cheesy umami; it is the backbone of 된장찌개, perhaps the most everyday Korean stew. The key verb is 풀다 (literally 'loosen'): because the paste is dense, you don't just drop it in, you stir it until it dissolves through the broth — 된장을 물에 풀다. Don't mix it up with red 고추장 (spicy chili paste) or with Japanese-style miso, which is milder and sweeter. 된장 collocates with 풀다, 끓이다, 넣다, and 으로/로 (cook WITH it). The English-speaker pitfall is the instrument particle: 된장으로 끓이다 (because 된장 ends in a consonant it takes 으로, not 로).

usage: 넣다 = add; 를 marks the vinegar
examples: I add a little vinegar to the cold noodles.
식초 한 숟가락 넣으면 더 새콤해요.
Add one spoon of vinegar and it gets tangier.
nuance: 식초 食醋 (literally 'food-vinegar') is sour vinegar used to give food a fresh, sharp tang. Its core taste word is 시다 (sour), but Koreans often prefer the softer, appetizing 새콤하다 ('pleasantly tangy'), which carries a positive nuance that plain 시다 lacks — vinegar in cold noodles or pickles is 새콤해요, not merely 셔요. It collocates with 넣다, 섞다, 치다 (splash vinegar on), and the flavor pair 새콤달콤 (sweet-and-sour). The English-speaker pitfall is conjugating 시다: the 요-form is 시어요/셔요, not 'sieyo' as a literal vowel-by-vowel reading might suggest, and learners often default to 'sour' = 시다 when describing dressed dishes, where 새콤하다 sounds far more natural and tasty.

examples: I sprinkle pepper on the meat.
에 marks the surface; 뿌리다 = scatter on top
This soup has a strong peppery taste.
at the table; bare noun + 좀
nuance: 후추 (originally from 호초 胡椒, 'foreign/barbarian pepper', reflecting that black pepper came via the Silk Road) is ground black pepper that gives a sharp, warm, slightly numbing pungency. The crucial contrast is 후추 (black pepper) versus 고추 (chili pepper) and 고춧가루 (chili powder): they sound alike to beginners but are botanically unrelated and taste different — 후추 is woody and aromatic, 고추 is fiery red heat. 후추 collocates with 뿌리다 (its signature verb — you sprinkle it on at the end), 넣다, 갈다 (grind), and 후추 맛/향 (pepper taste/aroma). The English-speaker pitfall is exactly the 후추/고추 mix-up, plus reaching for 넣다 when the natural finishing verb is 뿌리다, scattering it over the top.

usage: 만들다 = make; 을 marks the seasoning mix
I marinate it in the seasoning
재우다 = let marinate; 에 marks the bath
examples: Mom makes the marinade for the meat.
This seasoning is a bit spicy.
I marinate the chicken in the seasoning.
재우다 = leave to soak up flavor
nuance: 양념 is the native-Korean word for a whole blend of seasonings — soy sauce, garlic, sesame oil, sugar, chili — mixed to flavor a dish, NOT a single spice. This is the key contrast: one spice is a 향신료 or just its name (소금, 후추), but the prepared mixture you rub or pour on is 양념. The word also signals a style: 양념치킨 is chicken coated in sweet-spicy 양념 sauce, opposite 후라이드 (plain fried). 양념 collocates with 만들다 (make), 무치다 (toss/dress vegetables in it), 재우다 (marinate), 바르다 (brush on), and the verb 양념하다 (to season). The English-speaker pitfall is assuming 양념 = one spice; if you only added salt, that's not really 양념 — 양념 implies a composed blend, and you marinate IN it with 에 (양념에 재우다).

usage: 마시다 = drink; 을 marks the liquid
examples: I drank up all the ramyeon broth.
다 = all the way; 마시다 for liquid
hot soup that feels good going down
The broth is still hot, so be careful.
nuance: 국물 (국 'soup' + 물 'water') is the liquid part of a soup or stew, as opposed to the 건더기 (the solid pieces) — that pair is the contrast to know. Its most famous quirk is the word 시원하다: applied to a steaming hot broth, 시원해요 does NOT mean cold — it means the hot liquid feels refreshing, clearing, soothing, the way a hot bath or a sip of hot soup makes you exhale 'ahh'. 국물 collocates with 마시다 (drink — you drink broth, you don't 먹다 it), 우러나다 (flavor steeps out), 진하다 (rich/concentrated), and 시원하다/뜨겁다. The headline English-speaker pitfall is hearing 시원한 국물 and translating 'cold broth' — for liquid you actually drink, use 마시다, and read 시원하다 as 'soothing'.

Conjugating 뜨겁다 as 뜨겁어요. It is ㅂ-irregular: 뜨거워요.

examples: 로 marks flour as the material
I dissolve the flour in water.
밀가루 음식 = noodles, bread, dumplings, etc.
nuance: 밀가루 (밀 'wheat' + 가루 'powder') is specifically wheat flour. The compound is transparent — '가루' means any fine powder, so 쌀가루 is rice flour, 콩가루 bean powder, 고춧가루 chili powder — which means 밀가루 by itself always implies WHEAT, and you can't use it generically for 'flour' from other grains. Culturally, 밀가루 음식 (wheat-based food: noodles, bread, fritters) is a whole category often set against 밥 (rice meals). It collocates with 반죽하다 (knead into dough), 풀다 (dissolve into liquid), 묻히다 (coat food in flour), and 로 (made from flour). The English-speaker pitfall is using 밀가루 as a catch-all for 'flour': if it's rice flour you must say 쌀가루, and the material particle after the vowel-final 밀가루 is 로, not 으로.

usage: 넣다 = add; 을 marks the oil
examples: I add sesame oil to the bibimbap.
finishing touch; 에 marks the dish
This seasoned vegetable smells nicely of sesame oil.

nuance: 참기름 (참 'true/genuine' + 기름 'oil') is fragrant toasted sesame oil, prized for finishing dishes — added at the very end for aroma, not used for high-heat frying. Note the 참 prefix means 'true/real', distinguishing it from 들기름 (perilla oil), its closest cousin: both are nutty finishing oils, but 참기름 is from sesame and rounder, 들기름 from perilla leaves and grassier/sharper. Its signature taste word is 고소하다, that warm toasty-nutty quality English has no single word for. 참기름 collocates with 넣다, 두르다 (drizzle around), 바르다 (brush on seaweed/meat), and the aroma noun 향. Two pitfalls for English speakers: don't use 참기름 to deep-fry (it's a finishing oil, and it burns), and both partner verbs 두르다 and 바르다 are 르-irregular, becoming 둘러요 and 발라요.

mistakes: Using 참기름 to deep-fry. It's a finishing/aroma oil added at the end; use 식용유 for frying.
